In a strategic game, a **best response** of player $i$ to a list $a_{-i}$ of the other players' actions is an action that maximizes $i$'s payoff while the others' actions are held fixed. The **best-response correspondence** is
$$B_i(a_{-i}) = \{\, a_i\in A_i \;:\; u_i(a_i, a_{-i}) \ge u_i(a_i', a_{-i}) \text{ for all } a_i'\in A_i \,\}.$$
$B_i(a_{-i})$ is nonempty when $A_i$ is finite (or compact with $u_i$ continuous in $a_i$), and it may contain several actions; when it is always a single action, $b_i(a_{-i})$ is called the **best-response function**. In a bimatrix, player 1's best responses to column $c$ are the rows holding the largest first entry of that column, and player 2's best responses to row $r$ are the columns holding the largest second entry of that row.

A **Nash equilibrium** of a strategic game is an action profile $a^*$ from which no player can gain by changing her own action while the others keep theirs:
$$u_i(a^*_i, a^*_{-i}) \;\ge\; u_i(a_i, a^*_{-i})\qquad\text{for every player } i \text{ and every action } a_i\in A_i.$$
Equivalently $a^*_i\in B_i(a^*_{-i})$ for every $i$: each player's action is a best response to the others' — $a^*$ is a fixed point of the best-response correspondence $a\mapsto B_1(a_{-1})\times\cdots\times B_n(a_{-n})$. In a bimatrix the (pure) Nash equilibria are the cells in which both entries are best replies. A game may have no pure equilibrium (game-1.6), exactly one (game-1.4) or several (game-1.5).

A **correlated equilibrium** of a finite game is a probability distribution $\mu$ on the set $A$ of action profiles such that, when a mediator draws $a\sim\mu$ and privately recommends $a_i$ to each player $i$, no player gains by disobeying: for every player $i$ and all actions $a_i,a_i'$,
$$\sum_{a_{-i}}\mu(a_i,a_{-i})\bigl[u_i(a_i,a_{-i})-u_i(a_i',a_{-i})\bigr]\ \ge\ 0 .$$
These are finitely many linear inequalities in $\mu$, so the set of correlated equilibria is a nonempty convex polytope (a linear-programming feasible set, algo-11.15). Every Nash equilibrium is one (take $\mu$ a product distribution), as is every convex combination of Nash equilibria; but the polytope is generally larger, and can contain outcomes with higher payoffs than any Nash equilibrium.

Every finite strategic game — finitely many players, each with finitely many actions, arbitrary payoffs — has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies. Equivalently, the product of simplices $\Delta=\prod_i\Delta(A_i)$ contains a profile $\sigma^*$ such that $U_i(\sigma^*)\ge U_i(\tau_i,\sigma^*_{-i})$ for every player $i$ and every mixed $\tau_i$. Nash's second proof defines the continuous map $f:\Delta\to\Delta$,
$$f(\sigma)_{i}(a)=\frac{\sigma_i(a)+g_i^a(\sigma)}{1+\sum_{b}g_i^b(\sigma)},\qquad g_i^a(\sigma)=\max\bigl\{0,\;U_i(a,\sigma_{-i})-U_i(\sigma)\bigr\},$$
whose fixed points are exactly the equilibria; Brouwer's theorem gives a fixed point. Existence is all that is asserted: the equilibrium need not be unique, and iterating $f$ need not converge to it.

Let $A$ be a finite real $m\times n$ zero-sum payoff matrix, with the row player maximizing and the column player minimizing. Start cumulative action counts at $r_0=0$, $c_0=0$. In **simultaneous fictitious play**, round $t\ge1$ chooses
$$\begin{aligned}i_t&\in\arg\max_i(Ac_{t-1})_i,\\j_t&\in\arg\min_j(r_{t-1}^{\mathsf T}A)_j,\\r_t&=r_{t-1}+e_{i_t},\\c_t&=c_{t-1}+e_{j_t}.\end{aligned}$$
Zero initial scores make the first choices arbitrary; no frequency at time zero is needed. Robinson also treats the **alternating** rule: choose the same $i_t$ first, update $r_t$, then choose $j_t\in\arg\min_j(r_t^{\mathsf T}A)_j$. Either rule allows any choice among tied best replies. Put $\bar x_t=r_t/t$, $\bar y_t=c_t/t$, $g(x)=\min_j(x^{\mathsf T}A)_j$, and $h(y)=\max_i(Ay)_i$. **Robinson's theorem (1951)** says, for either timing,
$$h(\bar y_t)-g(\bar x_t)\;\longrightarrow\;0\quad(t\to\infty),$$
so $g(\bar x_t)\le v\le h(\bar y_t)$ converge to the minimax value $v$ (game-3.3). Every limit point of the empirical pair is optimal; equivalently, its distance to the product of optimal-strategy sets tends to zero. This does not assert convergence to one particular optimal pair, convergence of the actions, monotonicity of either bound, or a convergence rate.

A learner repeatedly chooses a mixed strategy $x_t$ over $m$ actions; then an arbitrary gain vector $g_t\in[0,1]^m$ is revealed. The **multiplicative weights (Hedge)** rule plays $x_t(i)\propto\exp\bigl(\eta\sum_{s<t}g_s(i)\bigr)$. Its **regret** against the best fixed action,
$$R_T=\max_i\sum_{t\le T}g_t(i)-\sum_{t\le T}x_t\cdot g_t,$$
satisfies $R_T\le\dfrac{\ln m}{\eta}+\dfrac{\eta T}{8}$ for every sequence $g_1,\dots,g_T$ (adaptive or not), hence $R_T\le\sqrt{T\ln m/2}$ for $\eta=\sqrt{8\ln m/T}$: the average regret vanishes like $T^{-1/2}$. In a zero-sum game with payoffs scaled into $[0,1]$, if both players run Hedge, the time-averaged strategies $\bar x_T,\bar y_T$ form an $\varepsilon$-approximate minimax pair with
$$\varepsilon=\max_i(A\bar y_T)_i-\min_j(\bar x_T^{\mathsf T}A)_j\le\frac{R_T^{\rm row}+R_T^{\rm col}}{T}=O\!\bigl(\sqrt{\ln(mn)/T}\bigr),$$
which gives a constructive proof of the minimax theorem (game-3.3).
fields.after:
